To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the brain abnormalities in FASD are related to facial dysmorphologies, that the callosal thickness reductions are related to facial abnormalities, and that the callosa are abnormal.
the thickness of callosal subregions is reduced and that the degree of reduction is associated with the degree of facial dysmorphology and with IQ.

the callosal thickness in the fetal alcohol spectrum disorders group is reduced in the anterior and posterior midbody, and that the callosa of individuals with fetal alcohol syndrome are thinner than those with partial fetal alcohol syndrome.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of facial dysmorphology and the neurobiological underpinnings of this phenotype.
the effects of alcohol on the human brain and its behavioral correlates.
how the brain and behavior develop and are affected by prenatal alcohol exposure in humans.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is sufficient evidence for a relationship between prenatal alcohol exposure (FAE) and neurodevelopmental disorders, and that the severity of the disorder is related to the amount of alcohol consumed.
there are no known teratogenic effects of alcohol in pregnancy.
there is a strong evidence base for fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) and fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) as well as the effects of prenatal alcohol exposure in the absence of FAS/FASD.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated the utility of callosal thickness as a marker of brain injury in fetal alcohol spectrum disorder.
the callosal thickness reductions in FASD are associated with facial dysmorphology.
the thickness of callosal subregions is reduced in FASD and these reductions relate to facial anomalies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need to be more aware of the potential for alcohol use during pregnancy to affect the developing brain.
there is a relationship between the thickness of the corpus callosum and the severity of dysmorphology, and that this relationship can be seen even before birth.
the brain is a dynamic organ and that the brain of an individual with FASD is not static.
